# Statement of Need

Adult literacy remains one of the most persistent and least visible barriers to economic mobility in the United States. Nationally, approximately 21% of adults read at or below a fifth-grade level (National Center for Education Statistics, [YEAR]), yet public investment in adult basic education has declined in real dollars over the past decade. In [CITY/COUNTY], the consequences of this gap are not abstract — they shape who can hold a job, navigate a lease, help a child with homework, or understand a medical diagnosis.

**The local picture is stark.** According to [LOCAL DATA SOURCE, YEAR], an estimated [X]% of adults in [TARGET NEIGHBORHOOD(S)] lack functional literacy skills, a rate [X] times the statewide average of [X]%. This concentration is not coincidental. The neighborhoods we serve have experienced decades of disinvestment: median household income sits at $[X] (American Community Survey, [YEAR]), [X]% of residents lack a high school diploma or equivalency, and unemployment runs [X] percentage points above the citywide rate. Low literacy is both a product of these conditions and a force that deepens them.

**The problem is not improving — it is compounding.** Between [YEAR] and [YEAR], [RELEVANT INDICATOR — e.g., adult education enrollment, GED completion rates, workforce participation among adults without credentials] in [CITY/COUNTY] [declined/stagnated] by [X]% ([SOURCE]). The COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted the limited programming that did exist: [X] adult education providers in the region reduced capacity or closed permanently between 2020 and [YEAR] ([SOURCE OR INTERNAL SCAN]). At the same time, demand has grown. Employers in [CITY/COUNTY]'s largest sectors — [SECTORS, e.g., healthcare, logistics, manufacturing] — increasingly require digital literacy and written communication skills that adults reading below a sixth-grade level cannot demonstrate, effectively locking our residents out of [X]% of posted positions ([WORKFORCE BOARD OR LABOR DATA, YEAR]).

**Existing services cannot meet the need.** [CITY/COUNTY] currently has [X] publicly funded adult literacy programs serving a combined [X] learners per year, against an estimated need of [X] ([SOURCE]). The nearest program to our target neighborhoods is [X] miles away and operates only during daytime hours, creating transportation and scheduling barriers for working adults and caregivers. [ORGANIZATION NAME] is the only provider offering [KEY DIFFERENTIATOR — e.g., evening and weekend classes, multilingual instruction, integrated digital literacy, neighborhood-based delivery] within [GEOGRAPHIC AREA]. Even so, our current capacity cannot keep pace with demand: as of [DATE], [X] adults are on our program waitlist, with an average wait time of [X] weeks.

**Residents confirm what the data show.** In a community needs survey conducted in [MONTH YEAR] (n=[X]), [X]% of respondents identified reading and writing skills as the single greatest barrier to employment or career advancement. One respondent wrote, "[DIRECT QUOTE — e.g., 'I can do the work, but I can't fill out the application. I can't even read the safety manual they hand you on the first day.']" These voices echo what our intake staff hear weekly: adults who are resourceful, motivated, and capable, but locked out of opportunity by a skill gap that targeted instruction can close.

The need is clear, it is growing, and existing resources are insufficient. [ORGANIZATION NAME] is positioned to respond — but only with the capacity this funding would provide.

---

## Suggested Data Sources

Pull your local numbers from these — they will give you the most credible, reviewer-friendly citations:

1. **National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) — Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC).** National and some state-level adult literacy/numeracy rates. Good for your opening national benchmark.
2. **U.S. Census Bureau — American Community Survey (ACS), 5-Year Estimates.** Neighborhood-level income, educational attainment, language spoken at home, employment. Use the most recent 5-year release for small-area data.
3. **Your state's Department of Education or Adult Education office.** Enrollment, completion, and waitlist data for federally funded adult education (WIOA Title II). Often published in annual reports.
4. **Your local Workforce Development Board or American Job Center.** Job posting requirements, employer skill demands, labor market data for your region. Many publish annual labor market analyses.
5. **National Coalition for Literacy or ProLiteracy — annual reports.** Useful for national trend context and service-gap framing.
6. **Your own program data.** Waitlist length, intake demographics, survey results, referral sources. Funders value primary data because it shows you are listening and tracking.

When you're ready, I can move on to the Target Population section or any other piece of the skeleton.

# Target Population

[ORGANIZATION NAME] will serve [X] adults per year, reaching [X] individuals over the [X]-year grant period. Our learners are adults aged 18 and older living in [TARGET NEIGHBORHOOD(S)/ZIP CODE(S)] within [CITY/COUNTY] who read at or below a [X]-grade level, as measured by a standardized intake assessment ([TABE, CASAS, or OTHER TOOL]). We prioritize those who face the steepest barriers to accessing existing services — working adults, caregivers, individuals with limited English proficiency, and residents without reliable transportation.

**Our learners reflect the communities we serve.** Based on [YEAR] program data, [X]% of participants identify as [RACE/ETHNICITY], [X]% as [RACE/ETHNICITY], and [X]% as [RACE/ETHNICITY]. Approximately [X]% are women, [X]% are parents or primary caregivers of minor children, and [X]% speak a language other than English at home ([PRIMARY LANGUAGES]). Household income among participants averages $[X] annually, and [X]% fall at or below [X]% of the federal poverty level.

**This population is underserved by design, not by choice.** The [X] existing adult literacy programs in [CITY/COUNTY] operate during standard business hours in locations that require [X]-minute commutes by public transit from our target neighborhoods ([SOURCE/INTERNAL ANALYSIS]). For adults juggling shift work, childcare, and limited transportation, these programs are functionally inaccessible. The result is a population that is simultaneously highest-need and hardest to reach — precisely the learners [ORGANIZATION NAME] was built to serve.

Eligibility is confirmed at intake through a brief verification process. Each prospective learner completes the following before enrollment:

1. Photo ID confirming age 18 or older
2. Proof of residence in [TARGET ZIP CODE(S)/NEIGHBORHOOD(S)] (utility bill, lease, or similar document)
3. Self-reported household income screened against [X]% FPL threshold
4. Standardized literacy assessment ([TABE/CASAS/OTHER]) administered on-site
5. Brief intake interview documenting goals, barriers, scheduling needs, and language preference
6. Signed program participation agreement and data consent form
7. Emergency contact and optional demographic self-identification form

Staff complete verification within [X] business days of initial contact to minimize dropout between inquiry and enrollment — a critical retention point that our [YEAR] data shows accounts for [X]% of lost learners.

# Program Design & Activities

## Logic Model Summary

[ORGANIZATION NAME]'s program rests on a straightforward theory of change: when adults who lack functional literacy receive sustained, contextualized instruction in a neighborhood-based setting with wraparound support, they gain the reading, writing, and digital skills needed to pursue employment, further education, and fuller participation in civic and family life. This theory is grounded in adult learning research demonstrating that skill acquisition among low-literacy adults requires a minimum of [X] hours of direct instruction to produce measurable gains ([SOURCE — e.g., National Research Council, NCSALL, or similar]) and that retention improves dramatically when programs reduce logistical barriers such as transportation, childcare, and rigid scheduling ([SOURCE]).

The logic model, attached as [ATTACHMENT LABEL], follows this chain:

- **Inputs:** [X] FTE instructors, [X] trained volunteers, classroom space at [X] neighborhood sites, curriculum ([NAME/TYPE]), assessment tools ([TABE/CASAS/OTHER]), grant and leveraged funding totaling $[X]
- **Activities:** Core Literacy Instruction, Digital Literacy Labs, and Transition & Follow-Up Services (described in detail below)
- **Outputs:** [X] adults enrolled per year, [X] instructional hours delivered per cohort, [X] digital literacy workshops completed, [X] individualized transition plans created
- **Short-term outcomes (0–6 months):** Participants increase reading level by at least [X] grade levels as measured by [ASSESSMENT TOOL]; [X]% demonstrate basic digital competency on [MEASURE]
- **Medium-term outcomes (6–12 months):** [X]% of completers obtain employment, enroll in further education/training, or earn a [GED/credential]; [X]% report increased confidence managing daily literacy tasks (self-report survey)
- **Long-term outcomes (1–3 years):** Sustained employment or educational enrollment; increased household income; intergenerational literacy engagement
- **External factors/assumptions:** Participants remain in the service area; employer demand for entry-level workers continues; partner organizations maintain referral capacity

---

## Core Activities

### Activity 1: Core Literacy Instruction

Each cohort of [X] learners participates in [X] weeks of small-group literacy instruction, meeting [X] times per week for [X] hours per session ([X] total contact hours per cohort). Classes are held at [SITE(S) — e.g., community center, library branch, church fellowship hall] in [TARGET NEIGHBORHOOD(S)], within walking distance or one bus transfer for [X]% of participants. Instruction is delivered by [X] credentialed adult education instructors (qualifications: [DEGREE/CERTIFICATION]) supported by [X] trained volunteer tutors at a ratio of no more than [X] learners per instructor.

The curriculum ([NAME OR TYPE — e.g., evidence-based managed enrollment model, contextualized workforce literacy, integrated English literacy and civics]) uses real-world materials — job applications, lease agreements, prescription labels, school correspondence — to anchor skill-building in the tasks learners need to perform daily. This directly addresses the functional literacy gap and employment barriers documented in the Statement of Need. Research supports contextualized instruction as more effective than generic skill-and-drill approaches for adult learners, producing [X]% greater gains in reading comprehension over comparable timeframes ([SOURCE, YEAR]).

### Activity 2: Digital Literacy Labs

Low literacy and low digital fluency overlap almost entirely in our target population. In our [YEAR] intake data, [X]% of incoming learners had never used email and [X]% could not complete an online job application without assistance. To address this gap, each cohort receives [X] hours of hands-on digital literacy instruction, delivered in [X]-hour weekly lab sessions running concurrently with the core literacy cycle. Labs are facilitated by [POSITION TITLE] using [CURRICULUM/PLATFORM — e.g., Northstar Digital Literacy, DigitalLearn.org, or locally developed modules] and held in [LOCATION — e.g., on-site computer lab with X stations].

Content progresses from foundational skills (using a mouse, navigating a browser, creating an email account) to applied tasks (online job searches, completing digital forms, accessing public benefits portals). This activity responds directly to the workforce data cited in the Statement of Need showing that [X]% of entry-level postings in [CITY/COUNTY] require basic digital competency ([SOURCE, YEAR]).

### Activity 3: Transition & Follow-Up Services

Instruction alone does not close the opportunity gap. Beginning at the midpoint of each cohort cycle, [POSITION TITLE — e.g., Transition Navigator, Case Manager] works individually with each learner to develop a written transition plan identifying next steps — employment, GED enrollment, vocational training, or continued literacy advancement — along with concrete action items and referrals to partner organizations ([PARTNER NAMES]). Each learner receives at least [X] one-on-one sessions before program exit.

After completion, staff conduct follow-up contact at [X] months and [X] months post-exit via phone, text, or in-person check-in to track progress, troubleshoot barriers, and reconnect learners to services as needed. This follow-up loop directly addresses the retention and dropout patterns identified in the Statement of Need, where [X]% of adults who leave programming without a structured transition do not re-engage within [X] months ([SOURCE OR INTERNAL DATA]).

---

## Participant Pathway

Every learner follows a defined pathway from first contact to follow-up. Prospective participants are referred by [REFERRAL SOURCES — e.g., workforce centers, schools, health clinics, self-referral] or drawn from the program waitlist. Within [X] business days, staff complete the intake verification process described in the Target Population section, administer the baseline literacy assessment, and assign the learner to the next available cohort. During the [X]-week instructional cycle, learners participate in Core Literacy Instruction and Digital Literacy Labs simultaneously. At the cycle midpoint, the Transition Navigator begins individualized planning. At program exit, staff administer a post-assessment, finalize the transition plan, and schedule follow-up contacts. Learners who have not met their goals may re-enroll for one additional cycle with instructor approval.

---

## Cohort Management

[ORGANIZATION NAME] operates on a managed-enrollment cohort model, launching [X] cohorts of [X] learners per [YEAR/QUARTER/SEMESTER] across [X] sites. Managed enrollment — in which a cohort begins and ends together rather than accepting rolling admissions — is supported by research as more effective for building classroom community and enabling sequential curriculum delivery ([SOURCE]). Cohort start dates are staggered by [X] weeks across sites so that waitlisted adults are never more than [X] weeks from an available seat.

---

## Risks and Mitigation

The primary program risk is participant attrition, which runs between [X]% and [X]% in comparable adult literacy programs nationally ([SOURCE]). We mitigate this through the design features described above — neighborhood-based delivery, flexible scheduling (evening and weekend options at [X] sites), childcare support through [PARTNER OR INTERNAL ARRANGEMENT], and proactive outreach when a learner misses [X] consecutive sessions. A secondary risk is instructor turnover. We address this by maintaining a trained volunteer bench of [X] tutors who can sustain instruction during hiring gaps and by offering competitive compensation benchmarked to [SALARY SOURCE/STANDARD]. [ORGANIZATION NAME] reviews attrition and staffing data quarterly and adjusts recruitment, scheduling, and support services in response.

---

Ready to move to Staffing & Implementation Timeline, or would you rather jump to another section?

# Outcomes & Objectives

## Outputs vs. Outcomes

Before presenting objectives, it is important to distinguish outputs from outcomes, as reviewers weight them differently. Outputs measure what the program delivers — the number of learners enrolled, instructional hours provided, workshops held. Outcomes measure what changes for learners as a result — skill gains, employment, continued education. The objectives below are outcome-focused. Output targets (e.g., [X] learners enrolled per year, [X] instructional hours delivered per cohort, [X] digital literacy labs completed) are tracked internally and reported in progress narratives but are not substitutes for evidence of learner change.

---

## SMART Objectives

### Objective 1: Literacy Skill Gain

By the end of each [X]-week cohort cycle, at least [X]% of participants who complete the program will improve their reading level by a minimum of [X] grade levels, as measured by pre- and post-administration of the [TABE/CASAS/OTHER], compared with a baseline average intake reading level of [X] grade equivalent ([YEAR program data or pilot results]).

**Why this matters:** The Statement of Need documented that [X]% of adults in [TARGET NEIGHBORHOOD(S)] lack functional literacy skills. A [X]-grade-level gain moves learners across the threshold from survival-level reading into functional literacy, enabling them to navigate employment applications, health information, and educational materials independently.

### Objective 2: Digital Competency

By the end of each cohort cycle, at least [X]% of participants will demonstrate basic digital competency — defined as the ability to use email, conduct a web search, and complete an online form — as measured by the [Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment / OTHER TOOL] post-test, up from a baseline of [X]% at intake ([YEAR program data]).

**Why this matters:** Workforce data cited in the Statement of Need show that [X]% of entry-level positions in [CITY/COUNTY] require digital skills that our learners currently lack ([SOURCE, YEAR]). This objective directly targets the digital barrier that locks residents out of available employment.

### Objective 3: Employment, Education, or Training Placement

Within [X] months of program completion, at least [X]% of program completers will have obtained employment, enrolled in a GED or vocational training program, or enrolled in a next-level adult education course, up from a baseline placement rate of [X]% among similar learners not receiving transition support ([YEAR internal data or comparable program data, SOURCE]).

**Why this matters:** Instruction without a structured bridge to next steps produces skill gains that often stall. This objective measures whether the Transition Navigator pathway described in Activity 3 converts literacy improvement into tangible economic or educational progress.

### Objective 4: Learner Confidence and Self-Efficacy

By program exit, at least [X]% of completers will report increased confidence in managing daily literacy and digital tasks (e.g., reading mail, helping children with schoolwork, using public benefits portals), as measured by a pre/post self-efficacy survey using a validated [X]-point Likert scale, compared with baseline scores collected at intake.

**Why this matters:** Community voice data from our [YEAR] needs survey showed that [X]% of respondents identified low confidence — not just low skill — as a barrier to pursuing employment and education. Sustainable change requires that learners internalize their own capability, and capturing this dimension ensures the program addresses the whole person rather than a test score alone.

---

## Measurement Tools and Timing

| Objective | Tool | Administered By | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Literacy Skill Gain | [TABE / CASAS / OTHER] — standardized, nationally normed | Lead Literacy Instructor | Pre: intake week. Post: final week of cohort cycle. Optional midpoint at week [X] for formative use. |
| 2. Digital Competency | [Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment / OTHER] | Digital Literacy Facilitator | Pre: first lab session. Post: final lab session. |
| 3. Employment/Education Placement | Staff-administered follow-up survey supplemented by third-party verification (employer confirmation, enrollment letter, or partner-agency report) | Transition Navigator | [X] months and [X] months post-exit. |
| 4. Learner Confidence | [X]-item self-efficacy survey ([validated instrument name or internally developed, pilot-tested in YEAR]) | Program Assistant (to separate assessment from instruction) | Pre: intake. Post: final week. Optional follow-up at [X]-month check-in. |

All data are entered into [DATA SYSTEM — e.g., Salesforce, ETO, Apricot, internal database] within [X] business days of collection. The Program Director reviews outcome dashboards quarterly and shares findings with staff, the board, and the funder per the reporting schedule outlined in the Evaluation Plan.

---

Ready for the Evaluation Plan, or would you like to jump to another section?

But if you'd rather tackle the Budget Narrative, Organizational Capacity, Sustainability Plan, or Executive Summary instead, we can go in whatever order works for you.
